name: Napier's rods
where: The visitor is at one of the rod stations (rods 2–7): a tall column shaped like a giant Napier's rod, with a square screen in front and a small table below with a tray for three rods, an LED grid under the tray and a display that shows a problem. The screen pages through six steps: Napier's rods (rods 1, 4, 7, 9); one rod, one table (rod 7, row 3: 7 × 3 = 21); line up the number (rods 4, 2, 5 side by side make 425); find the row (425 × 6, row 6 reads 24, 12, 30); add the diagonals (2, 5, 5, 0 → 2550); and 'Your turn' (rods 3, 8, 6), pointing to the rods on the table below. A seventh page shows a 3D model of a real set in its wooden box (sixteen rods on a tray that slides into a case with a sliding lid); visitors double-tap to unpack it and drag the pieces around. On the table, a rod in the right slot lights green and a wrong one blinks amber; when all three are right the multiplier's row lights white, and holding the button for two seconds shows the answer.

presets.question: Why are they called bones?
presets.focus: The rods were commonly made of bone, ivory or boxwood, hence 'Napier's bones'. Each face carries one digit's multiplication table, written in squares split by a diagonal.

presets.question: How do the diagonals work?
presets.focus: Each square holds a product with the tens above the diagonal and the units below. Read the row for the multiplier and add along the diagonals (slants) from right to left, carrying. Use the screen's example: 425 × 6, row 6 reads 24, 12, 30, and the diagonals give 2 5 5 0 = 2550.

presets.question: Can the rods multiply two big numbers?
presets.focus: One reading multiplies a many-digit number by ONE digit. For a many-digit multiplier, take one reading per digit and add the results, shifted by place. Do not claim the rods do it in one reading.

presets.question: Why did you make them?
presets.focus: Long multiplication was slow, error-prone drudgery for astronomers, surveyors and merchants; the rods turn it into reading and adding. Rabdologia (1617) published them, the year he died.

presets.question: Did people really use them?
presets.focus: Sets were made for decades after 1617, in boxwood and later brass, and the rods travelled as far as China: Giacomo Rho's Chou Suan (1628) adapted Rabdologia into Chinese. He may speak of this as something he has been told since.

name: The Promptuarium
where: The visitor is at rod 15, the promptuary wall, with a tall screen of seven pages beside it. The wall: a number board with 98765 fixed on it (columns 9 8 7 6 5, four rows; every square holds its digit's whole times table in Napier's layout, tens above the slant and units below), and nine black plates ×1 to ×9 on a plate rail. A visitor lifts the plate for a digit of the multiplier and hooks it across a row, tab at the board's left edge; the plate's two windows per square show only that digit's answers. One plate per row, top row first; four rows allow up to a four-digit multiplier. Then the visitor adds the slanted bands from right to left, carrying. Napier's own strips and plates and the Madrid cabinet are on the wall graphic opposite, not on this screen.

pages.title: The Promptuarium
pages.screen: Napier’s last invention · Rabdologia, 1617 / plate 7 hung over the number 98765 / Napier’s rods still leave you writing down a partial product for every digit. The promptuarium skips that step. Number strips and window plates are laid across each other, so only the digits you need show through — then you just add. / in Rabdologia, Napier’s last book / partial products to write down / the only sum you do: adding small digits / THE REAL OBJECT / Napier’s own strips and plates, and the rare cabinet in Madrid, are on the wall graphic opposite. This screen shows how to use the number board and black plates. / HOW TO USE THE WALL / Meet the wall / board, plates, rows / Pick a plate / one plate per digit / Hang it across a row / only the answers show / Add along the slants / right to left / Two plates, bigger numbers / 98765 × 73 / Your turn / four challenges

pages.title: Meet the wall
pages.screen: Three parts, all in front of you / PLATE RAIL / four rows / The number board / 98765 is already set, one column per digit. Every square holds that digit’s whole times table, ×0 to ×9: tens above the slant, units below it. / The plates / Nine black plates, ×1 to ×9, hang on the rail beside the board. Each one has two windows per square, cut exactly where its own answer sits. / The rows / Hang one plate per row. One plate multiplies by one digit; with four rows you can multiply by a number up to four digits long. / the 7 square, close up / Where does 7 × 7 live? Its tens digit 4 sits above the slant, its units digit 9 below. Plate 7’s windows open on exactly those two boxes — in every square on the board.

pages.title: Step 1 · Pick a plate
pages.screen: One plate for each digit you multiply by / PLATE RAIL / Decide what to multiply 98765 by. For × 7, lift plate 7 off the rail. The digit is printed on the plate’s end tab; hold it by the edges. / WHY ONE PLATE FITS EVERY COLUMN / Napier put each answer in the same place in every square. The 7-times answer is always in these two boxes, so one plate finds it in all five columns at once: 63 56 49 42 35. / PLAN YOUR PLATES / 98765 × 7 / plate 7 / 98765 × 73 / plates 7 and 3, top to bottom / 98765 × 425 / plates 4, 2 and 5, top to bottom

pages.title: Step 2 · Hang it across
pages.screen: Only the 7-times answers stay visible / WHAT YOU SEE THROUGH THE WINDOWS / 9 × 7 / 8 × 7 / 7 × 7 / 6 × 7 / 5 × 7 / Hook plate 7 over the top row with its tab at the left edge. Everything else is covered: no hunting through a times table, no chance of reading the wrong line. / Each column now shows its digit × 7 — the tens digit above the slant, the units digit below. / TIP / Any row works for a single plate; the top row is easiest to reach. For two or more plates, start at the top and fill the rows in order. / IF SOMETHING LOOKS WRONG / Digit on the tab upside down? Turn the plate over — the tab goes on the left. Windows not on the numbers? Slide the plate until its tab sits against the board’s left edge.

pages.title: Step 3 · Add the slants
pages.screen: Right to left, one band at a time / 98765 × 7 = 691,355 / READ THE BANDS FROM THE RIGHT / 1st / 2nd / 3 + 2 / 3rd / 4 + 9 / write 3, carry 1 / 4th / 4 + 6 + 1 / write 1, carry 1 / 5th / 5 + 3 + 1 / 6th / WHY IT’S EASY / Each band holds two digits at most, plus a carry — sums small enough for your head. Write each answer digit to the left of the last one. / QUICK CHECK / 98765 is just under 100,000, so × 7 should land just under 700,000. 691,355 fits.

pages.title: Two plates, bigger numbers
pages.screen: 98765 × 73 · one row per digit / the seven bands, left to right / Hang the plate for the first digit (7) in the top row and the next digit (3) right below it. The slanted bands run straight through both rows, so tens and units line up by themselves — add each band exactly as before. / 1 + 8 + 5 / write 4, carry 1 / 1 + 3 + 1 + 2 + 1 / 2 + 4 + 4 + 9 / write 9, carry 1 / 2 + 4 + 7 + 6 + 1 / write 0, carry 2 / 2 + 5 + 3 + 2 / write 2, carry 1 / 6 + 1 / 98765 × 73 = 7,209,845 / carries are shown inside the sums · four rows = up to four digits

pages.title: Your turn
pages.screen: The plates are on the rail — try these / ONE PLATE / 98765 × 4 / Hang plate 4 in the top row. / answer, upside down: / ONE PLATE / 98765 × 9 / Plate 9. Look at all those eights. / answer, upside down: / TWO PLATES / 98765 × 25 / Plate 2 on top, plate 5 below it. / answer, upside down: / TWO PLATES / 98765 × 12 / Plate 1 on top, plate 2 below it. / answer, upside down: / Stuck on a band? Tap Napier and tell him which digits you can see. When you’re done, hang the plates back on the rail for the next visitor.

name: Location arithmetic
where: The visitor is at rod 16, the location arithmetic room, with a tall screen of eight pages. The floor is an L: the near strip worth 8 4 2 1 is the first number, the strip running toward the wall worth 1 2 4 8 is the second number, and START is the corner pad. Standing still on a square for 3 seconds switches it on (green); stepping off and standing there again for 3 seconds switches it off; each square switches once per visit. Standing on START for 3 seconds runs the multiplication: counters appear on the wall board where the two numbers cross, slide down-left along the diagonals to the bottom row and merge (two on one square make one on the next), and the answer flies back to the floor sum (the equation is on the floor, not on the wall). It stays a few seconds, then the floor clears. Each strip makes 1 to 15, so the biggest product is 15 × 15 = 225. Two people can play, one strip each. Napier's letters and the history of binary are on the wall graphics nearby, not on this screen.

pages.title: Location Arithmetic
pages.screen: Napier’s chessboard · Rabdologia, 1617 / the wall board working out 9 × 12 / Napier’s third way to calculate needs no times tables at all. Every square on his board is worth double the one beside it. Numbers are made of counters, and multiplying is just sliding them along the diagonals. / — Napier, on his board / 1 2 4 8 / every square doubles / times tables to remember / 3 s / stand still to choose a square / THE STORY / Napier’s letters a, b, c… and how his board became binary are on the wall graphics nearby. This screen shows you how to play the floor. / HOW TO PLAY / How the squares count / 8 + 1 = 9 / Meet the floor / strips, START, wall / Choose your first number / stand 3 seconds / Choose the second / the other strip / Stand on START / watch the wall / Watching the wall / slide and merge / Your turn / four challenges

pages.title: How the squares count
pages.screen: Light the squares that add up to your number / 8 + 1 = 9 / Each strip on the floor has four squares, worth 8, 4, 2 and 1. A number is simply the squares you light, added up. Four squares make every number from 1 to 15 — each in exactly one way. / EVERY NUMBER YOU CAN MAKE / WHY IT DOUBLES / Napier’s rule: two of the same square make one of the next — 1 + 1 = 2, 2 + 2 = 4. So you never need a square twice, and the wall uses the same rule to carry.

pages.title: Meet the floor
pages.screen: Two strips, one START pad, and the wall / THE WALL / THE FLOOR, FROM ABOVE / a × b = _ / ↓ you enter from this side ↓ / Near strip — 8 4 2 1. Your first number. / Strip toward the wall — 1 2 4 8. Your second number. / START pad. Stand here to run the multiplication. / The wall board. Counters appear, slide and join up — this is the working. / The floor sum. Your numbers and the answer are written here.

pages.title: Step 1 · First number
pages.screen: Stand still on a square for 3 seconds / 3 s / stand still / NEAR STRIP / 9 × _ / the floor sum fills in as you go / Step onto a square on the near strip and stand still. After 3 seconds it fills green — that square is on. / Light as many as you need: 8 and 1 make 9. / Changed your mind? Step off, then stand on the square again for 3 seconds to switch it off. / TRY MAKING / 13 = 8 + 4 + 1 6 = 4 + 2 11 = 8 + 2 + 1 The full list is on page 2.

pages.title: Step 2 · Second number
pages.screen: Now the strip that runs toward the wall / 9 × 12 = _ / Do the same on the strip that runs toward the wall: 8 + 4 = 12. / Each square switches once per visit — step off before you choose the next one. / The floor sum now reads 9 × 12 = _. Check it before you go to START. / TWO PLAYERS / Playing with a friend? Take one strip each — then one of you steps onto START.

pages.title: Step 3 · Stand on START
pages.screen: Then watch the wall do the multiplying / 9 × 12 = 108 / 3 s / Stand on START for 3 seconds. A light runs from the pad up into the wall board. / Counters appear wherever your two numbers cross on the wall. / They slide down the diagonals to the bottom row and join up. / The answer flies back down to the floor: 9 × 12 = 108. / AFTERWARDS / The answer stays for a few seconds, then the floor clears for the next player.

pages.title: Watching the wall
pages.screen: What the counters are doing / 64 + 32 + 8 + 4 = 108 / CROSSING = ROW × COLUMN / Where the 8 row meets the 8 column the square is worth 64; 9 and 12 cross in four places. / SLIDE DOWN-LEFT / One step down halves a square, one step left doubles it — so a counter keeps its value all the way to the bottom row. / TWO MAKE ONE / Two counters on one square become one counter on the next: 4 + 4 = 8. That’s Napier’s carry. Try 6 × 7 to watch it happen. / read the bottom row: every counter is a square you add
